title: Google Adopts DPoP to Strengthen OAuth 2.0 Against Token Theft and Replay Attacks
gist: Google OAuth now supports DPoP for refresh tokens to bind them to client keys and blunt infostealer token replay; it does not cover session cookies (Device Bound Session Credentials is the answer) and is unsuitable for multi-agent delegation.

insights.claim: Traditional OAuth bearer tokens work on a finders-keepers model, leaving them exposed to infostealers such as RedLine and NodeStealer and to adversary-in-the-middle attacks.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Stolen-token replay is a core account-takeover vector driving demand for sender-constrained tokens.

insights.claim: DPoP binds tokens to a client-generated asymmetric key pair so a stolen token cannot be replayed without the private key.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler adoption pushes sender-constrained tokens toward mainstream.
insights.locator: To prevent this types of attacks

insights.claim: Google applies DPoP only to long-lived refresh tokens, leaving short-lived access tokens as bearer tokens to avoid per-request asymmetric verification overhead.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Shows the performance/security tradeoff hyperscalers accept.
insights.quote: the primary vector for persistent online impersonation
insights.locator: Google OAuth platform supports DPoP only for refresh tokens

insights.claim: DPoP adoption adds client burden: key generation, timestamp and nonce handling, header construction and DPoP proof JWTs.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Integration cost may slow third-party adoption.
insights.locator: adopting DPoP adds several client-side requirements

insights.claim: DPoP does not protect web session cookies, which stay vulnerable to infostealers; Google and WICG are developing Device Bound Session Credentials to bind cookies to hardware such as a TPM.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: DPoP plus DBSC form a defense-in-depth stack; watch for browser and identity-provider rollout.
insights.locator: While DPoP provides protection for API tokens

insights.claim: Google says DPoP is not appropriate for multi-agent workflows because delegation would require one agent to sign with another's private key, and recommends Google Cloud Secure Token Service token exchange instead.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Agent-to-agent delegation is an unsolved identity problem; STS-style exchange is the recommended pattern.
insights.locator: Google also notes that DPoP is not appropriate

insights.claim: Because the DPoP key lives client-side, security depends on the client; browser SPAs are not fully protected and IETF guidance recommends a Backend-for-Frontend pattern to keep tokens and keys out of the browser.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Browser-only apps remain the weak link.
insights.locator: Since the DPoP private key is stored client-side
